label: 1 John 1:1–4
text:
Four verbs climb in physical intensity: "heard" (akēkoamen) and "seen" (heōrakamen) are both perfect tense — heard and seen, and it remains so, a settled fact — while "looked upon" (etheasametha) is a careful, deliberate gazing, the same root behind "theater," and "handled" (epsēlaphēsan) is a tactile groping, the identical verb used of Thomas touching the risen Christ's wounds.

The escalation from hearing to touching is deliberate polemic — John is answering, before he has said anything else, any suggestion that the Word who "was made flesh" was less than fully, physically real.

"Manifested" (ephanerōthē) repeats twice in one breath, describing eternal life as something that stepped, visibly, into ordinary sight rather than remaining a private revelation.

"Declare" is apangellomen, "to report back, to announce" — the same word used of messengers returning from a battlefield with news, appropriate for men who are relaying what they personally witnessed rather than passing on hearsay.

"Fellowship" is koinōnian, shared partnership in a common life — and "full" (peplērōmenē) is perfect passive, a joy that has reached its complete measure and remains there, not merely topped up occasionally.
translation: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we gazed upon and our hands felt, concerning the Word of life — and the life was manifested, and we have seen, and are testifying, and are reporting to you the eternal life, which was with the Father, and was manifested to us — that which we have seen and heard we are reporting also to you, so that you also may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ. And these things we are writing, so that our joy may be completely full.

label: 1 John 1:5–7
text:
"No darkness at all" translates a doubled negative for emphasis in the Greek, skotia ouk estin en autō oudemia — literally "darkness is not in him, not even one bit" — a categorical, exceptionless denial.

"Walk" (peripatōmen) is present subjunctive, naming an entire manner of ongoing conduct, not a single step taken rightly or wrongly.

"Lie" and "do not the truth" run in strict grammatical parallel — falsehood is pictured equally as something said and something enacted, a claim contradicted by a life rather than merely by a statement.

"Cleanseth" is katharizei, present tense — a continuous, ongoing cleansing rather than a single completed transaction, matching the continuous "walking in the light" that stands as its condition.
translation: And this is the message which we have heard from him and are reporting to you: that God is light, and in him there is no darkness, none at all. If we say we have fellowship with him and are walking in the darkness, we are lying and are not doing the truth. But if we are walking in the light as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son is continually cleansing us from every sin.

label: 1 John 1:8–10
text:
"Confess" is homologōmen, built from homos ("same") and logos ("word") — literally "to say the same thing," agreeing with God's own verdict about our sin rather than merely admitting a fault by our own private reckoning.

"Faithful and just" (pistos kai dikaios) grounds forgiveness in God's consistent character and in a justice already satisfied elsewhere, not in mere leniency overlooking the matter.

"Cleanse" shifts here to an aorist subjunctive — a decisive, completed act of cleansing tied directly to the moment of confession, distinct from the continuous, present-tense cleansing already described in verse 7.

"Make him a liar" (pseustēn poioumen auton) is a startling reversal — to deny one's sin is not merely self-deception, as verse 8 says, but an implicit accusation leveled directly at God's own truthfulness.
translation: If we say we have no sin, we are deceiving ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous, so as to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. If we say we have not sinned, we are making him a liar, and his word is not in us.

label: 1 John 2:1–2
text:
"Little children" is teknia, a diminutive, affectionate term literally meaning "little born ones" — John's characteristic form of address, used repeatedly across this letter for his readers regardless of their actual age.

"Advocate" is paraklēton, "one called alongside" to help — the identical noun used of the Holy Spirit as "Comforter" in John's Gospel, here applied instead to Christ's ongoing legal defense of believers before the Father.

"Propitiation" is hilasmos, naming the means by which the offense of sin is dealt with and God's righteous response to it satisfied — the word carries both the turning-away of judgment and the removal of sin's guilt in a single term.

"Not for ours only" widens hilasmos beyond any private or national circle — the same single provision is declared sufficient, in principle, for the whole world, without qualification.
translation: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous one. And he himself is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for the whole world's.

label: 1 John 2:3–6
text:
"Know" translates ginōskomen, the verb of experiential, relational knowing rather than bare factual awareness — assurance of "knowing him" is tested here not by a feeling but by an ongoing pattern of obedience.

"Keep" is tērōmen, present subjunctive — a continuous guarding and observing, not a single act of compliance checked off once.

"Perfected" is teteleiōtai, perfect passive of teleioō, "to bring to its intended goal, to mature" — not flawlessness but completion, love reaching the maturity it was always meant to reach.

"Abideth" is menein, a central Johannine verb for continuous, settled dwelling — the same word carrying the weight of the vine-and-branches image in John's Gospel, here demanding that claimed abiding be matched by an actual walk resembling Christ's own.
translation: And by this we know that we have come to know him: if we are keeping his commandments. The one who says, I have come to know him, and is not keeping his commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But whoever is keeping his word, truly in this one the love of God has been perfected. By this we know that we are in him. The one who says he is abiding in him ought himself also to be walking just as that one walked.

label: 1 John 2:7–11
text:
The "old" commandment and the "new" commandment name the identical thing seen from two angles — old because it was given long before, in the law and in Jesus' own teaching; new because it has only now become true, in actual fact, in Christ's life and in the changed lives of believers.

"Is past" (paragetai) is present tense, describing the darkness as something actively, currently passing away, a process still underway rather than already finished.

"Stumbling" is skandalon, originally the trigger-stick of an animal trap — a life of love, John claims, contains no hidden mechanism waiting to catch and trip either the one who loves or those around him.

"Blinded" is etyphlōsen, aorist — a completed act with a continuing result: the darkness didn't merely dim this man's sight once, it left him, from that point forward, unable to see where he is even now going.
translation: Beloved, I am writing no new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word which you heard. Again, a new commandment I am writing to you, which thing is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away, and the true light is already shining. The one who says he is in the light, and is hating his brother, is in the darkness until now. The one who loves his brother is abiding in the light, and there is no cause for stumbling in him. But the one who hates his brother is in the darkness, and is walking in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

label: 1 John 2:12–14
text:
John addresses three groups twice each, first in the present tense (graphō, "I am writing") and then in the past (egrapsa, "I have written") — a rhetorical device gathering his whole spiritual family, at every stage of maturity, into one sustained appeal.

"Little children" (teknia and paidia, two related diminutives) are addressed on the ground of forgiveness already accomplished; "fathers" are addressed for having known "him that is from the beginning," an identical description given both times without variation.

"Young men" are commended for having "overcome" (nenikēkate, perfect tense) — a victory won and still, in the present, standing firm — tied specifically to the word of God "abiding" (menei, present tense) in them as an ongoing, resident strength.
translation: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven you because of his name. I am writing to you, fathers, because you have come to know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I have written to you, little ones, because you have come to know the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have come to know him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God is abiding in you, and you have overcome the evil one.

label: 1 John 2:15–17
text:
"World" (kosmos) here names an organized system of values opposed to God, not the physical planet — loving it is set in direct, exclusive opposition to loving the Father, as though the two loves could not occupy the same heart at once.

"Pride of life" translates alazoneia tou biou — alazoneia is a rare word for boastful, ostentatious arrogance, drawn from alazōn, a stock character in Greek comedy: the wandering charlatan who boasts of accomplishments and possessions he doesn't actually have.

"Passeth away" (paragetai) repeats, word for word, the same present-tense verb already used of darkness "passing away" in 2:8 — the world's entire system is placed in that identical, already-underway process of dissolution.

"Abideth for ever" closes the contrast with menei, the letter's key verb for permanent, settled dwelling — obedience to God's will is tied to the one thing in the passage that does not, and will not, pass.
translation: Do not love the world, nor the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything in the world — the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the ostentatious pride of life — is not from the Father, but is from the world. And the world is passing away, and its lust, but the one who does the will of God abides forever.

label: 1 John 2:18–23
text:
"Antichrist" (antichristos) is a term John himself appears to have coined — anti carrying the double sense of both "against" and "in place of," so the word names both an opponent of Christ and a substitute claiming his role.

"Went out from us" is exēlthan, aorist — a decisive, completed departure, and John reads the fact of their leaving itself as retrospective proof they never truly belonged, rather than as a fall from a status they once genuinely held.

"Unction" is chrisma, the anointing substance itself rather than the act of anointing — a deliberate wordplay against antichristos: over against every false "anti-anointed one," ordinary believers are themselves, by the Spirit, the genuinely anointed ones.

The chain of denials — denying the Son leaves a man without the Father also — insists the two cannot be separated even in theory: acknowledging one is, necessarily, acknowledging both, and denying one is denying both at once.
translation: Little children, it is the last hour, and just as you heard that antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have come; from this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us; but they went out so that it might be shown that they all are not of us. And you have an anointing from the Holy One, and you all know. I did not write to you because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth. Who is the liar, if not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, the one who denies the Father and the Son. Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either. The one who acknowledges the Son has the Father also.

label: 1 John 2:24–29
text:
"Seduce" translates planōntōn, "to lead astray, to cause to wander" — the same root family behind the modern "planet," a heavenly body whose path appears to wander against the fixed stars.

"Confidence" is parrēsian, originally a civic term for a free citizen's right to speak openly and without fear in the public assembly — believers are pictured with that same unrestrained boldness, not merely tolerated but free to speak, before Christ at his coming.

"Abideth in you" (menei en hymin) repeats menō a third time in a few short verses — the anointing's permanence, once received, is treated as settled fact needing only to be recognized, not a status requiring further human instruction to maintain.

"Born of him" (ex autou gegennētai) is perfect tense — a birth already accomplished and still, presently, defining what a person is, tying right conduct directly to an already-completed spiritual parentage rather than to effort alone.
translation: As for you, let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, you also will abide in the Son and in the Father. And this is the promise which he himself promised us: eternal life. I have written these things to you concerning those who are trying to deceive you. And as for you, the anointing which you received from him is abiding in you, and you have no need that anyone teach you; but as his anointing is teaching you concerning all things, and is true, and is not a lie, and just as it has taught you, abide in him. And now, little children, abide in him, so that if he should be manifested we may have confidence, and not shrink away from him in shame at his coming. If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who is doing righteousness has been begotten of him.

label: 1 John 3:1–3
text:
"What manner of" translates potapēn, an exclamatory word originally asking "from what foreign country?" — implying love so extraordinary it seems to have arrived from somewhere outside ordinary human experience altogether.

"Bestowed" is dedōken, perfect tense — a gift already given and, right now, still standing given, not a favor extended once and then withdrawn to memory.

"Doth not yet appear" (oupō ephanerōthē) admits real, unresolved mystery about the believer's future state, even while "we know" (oidamen), stated with flat confidence, that being "like him" (homoioi autō) is certain regardless of the details still hidden.

"Purifieth" is hagnizei, present tense — an ongoing, continuous self-purification, motivated specifically by this forward-looking hope rather than by present guilt or fear.
translation: Behold what manner of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God — and we are. Because of this the world does not know us, because it did not know him. Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been made manifest what we will be. We know that if he is manifested we will be like him, because we will see him just as he is. And everyone who has this hope fixed on him is continually purifying himself, just as that one is pure.

label: 1 John 3:4–10
text:
"Committeth sin" and "sinneth" both translate present participles, poiōn tēn hamartian and hamartanōn — describing habitual, continuous practice, a settled way of life, rather than a single sinful act; this grammatical point is what keeps this passage from contradicting 1:8's admission that no one is free of sin altogether.

"Transgresseth...transgression" render anomian, "lawlessness" — sin is defined here precisely as being without law, in open defiance of it, not merely as falling short.

"Take away" is arē, aorist subjunctive — to lift up bodily and carry off entirely, the sins removed rather than merely covered or excused.

"Seed" (sperma) names the divine nature implanted at the new birth, described as remaining, present tense, within the believer — the reason "cannot sin" (ou dynatai hamartanein) likewise means unable to keep on sinning habitually, not incapable of a single lapse.

"Sinneth from the beginning" applied to the devil sets the pattern this entire passage argues against: continuous, defining sin as an identity, contrasted point for point with continuous, defining righteousness as the mark of one born of God.
translation: Everyone who is practicing sin is also practicing lawlessness, and sin is lawlessness. And you know that that one was manifested so that he might take away sins, and in him there is no sin. Everyone who is abiding in him is not habitually sinning; everyone who is habitually sinning has not seen him, nor come to know him. Little children, let no one deceive you; the one who is practicing righteousness is righteous, just as that one is righteous. The one who is practicing sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. For this the Son of God was manifested: so that he might destroy the works of the devil. Everyone who has been begotten of God is not practicing sin, because his seed is abiding in him, and he is not able to keep on sinning, because he has been begotten of God. By this the children of God and the children of the devil are made evident: everyone who is not practicing righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who is not loving his brother.

label: 1 John 3:11–15
text:
"Message" is angelia, "an announcement, a proclamation" — a distinct word from the "commandment" used elsewhere in the letter, casting mutual love as breaking news rather than a standing rule.

"Slew" translates esphaxen, a violent verb properly used of slaughtering a sacrificial animal — not the ordinary word for killing, but butchering; John reaches for the harshest available term to describe fratricide.

"Passed" is metabebēkamen, perfect tense — a completed crossing-over from one realm into another, and the crosser now standing permanently on the far side rather than shuttling back and forth.

"Hateth his brother is a murderer" collapses the distance between an inward disposition and an outward act — hatred is treated as murder already committed in principle, following the same logic Jesus applies to anger in the Sermon on the Mount.
translation: Because this is the message which you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another; not as Cain was of the evil one and slaughtered his brother. And for what reason did he slaughter him? Because his own works were evil, and his brother's were righteous. Do not marvel, brothers, if the world is hating you. We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. The one who is not loving is abiding in death. Everyone who is hating his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.

label: 1 John 3:16–18
text:
"Laid down" is etheken, the identical verb used of the Good Shepherd laying down his life in John's Gospel — the same specific act of self-giving is presented here as the pattern, not merely the inspiration, for love among believers.

"World's good" translates ton bion tou kosmou — bios means one's livelihood, the material means of living, distinct from zōē, the word for life itself used everywhere else in this letter.

"Shutteth up" is klysē, present tense — a continuous, ongoing closing-off, describing a settled habit of withholding rather than a single hard-hearted moment.

"Bowels of compassion" (ta splanchna) names the inward organs, the ancient seat of the deepest feeling — the question "how dwelleth the love of God in him" assumes such love, if genuinely present, could not possibly leave those organs unmoved.
translation: By this we have come to know love: because that one laid down his life for us, and we ourselves ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. But whoever has the world's means of living, and sees his brother having need, and shuts off his heart of compassion from him, how is the love of God abiding in him? Little children, let us not be loving in word, nor with the tongue, but in deed and truth.

label: 1 John 3:19–24
text:
"Assure" is peisomen, future tense — a settling of the heart still to be accomplished by this reasoning, not an assurance already fully in hand before the argument is even made.

"Condemn" is kataginōskē, literally "to know against" — a present subjunctive, the heart's ongoing capacity to raise a case against itself, met by the reminder that God, who "knoweth all things," has the final and larger word.

"Confidence" repeats parrēsian, the civic term for a free citizen's open, unafraid speech before an assembly, already used at 2:28 — the same boldness, now grounded specifically in a clear conscience rather than in the future coming of Christ.

The single "commandment" (entolē) is described in two parts joined as one — believing on the Son's name and loving one another — refusing to treat correct belief and active love as separable requirements.

"Abideth in us" closes the chapter with menei a final time, now identified explicitly by "the Spirit which he hath given us" as the actual mechanism, not merely the metaphor, behind that abiding.
translation: By this we will convince our heart, whenever our heart condemns us, that God is greater than our heart and knows all things. Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask we are receiving from him, because we are keeping his commandments and are practicing the things pleasing before him. And this is his commandment: that we should believe on the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and should love one another, just as he gave commandment to us. And the one who is keeping his commandments is abiding in him, and he in him; and by this we know that he is abiding in us, from the Spirit whom he gave us.

label: 1 John 4:1–6
text:
"Try" is dokimazete, "to test, to examine" — the same dokim- family used elsewhere of testing gold or the genuineness of faith, applied here to spirits claiming divine origin.

"Confesseth" is homologei, the identical "say the same thing" verb already used of confessing sin in 1:9 — orthodox confession and honest confession of sin are, grammatically, the same act of agreement with a prior truth.

"Is come in the flesh" translates a perfect participle, elēlythota — not a past event now over, but a completed coming whose result, an actual, ongoing incarnate state, still stands; the test excludes any teaching that reduces Christ's humanity to a temporary appearance.

"Overcome" repeats nenikēkate, perfect tense, the identical victory-word already applied to the "young men" in 2:13-14 — a settled, standing triumph rather than a single won skirmish.

"Greater" is meizōn, the same comparative already used at 3:20 of God being greater than the accusing heart — here applied to the Spirit resident in believers set directly against the spirit at work in the world.
translation: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit which confesses Jesus Christ having come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit which does not confess Jesus is not from God; and this is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now already is in the world. You are from God, little children, and have overcome them, because greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world. They are from the world; because of this they speak from the world, and the world listens to them. We are from God. The one who knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.

label: 1 John 4:7–12
text:
"God is love" (ho theos agapē estin) is a definitional statement rather than a description among others — love is offered as God's very nature, the reality every other attribute of God expresses, not one quality he happens to possess alongside the rest.

"Only begotten" is monogenē, "unique, one of a kind" — the same word used at John 3:16, ruling out any sense of the Son as merely one among many divine emissaries.

"Not that we loved God, but that he loved us" reverses the expected order of any human religious instinct — love's origin is placed entirely on God's side, with human love toward him named, deliberately, as the secondary, responsive act.

"Perfected" is teteleiōmenē, perfect passive — love reaching, in mutual love among believers, its intended completion, an idea this chapter will return to twice more before it ends.
translation: Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who is loving has been begotten of God and knows God. The one who is not loving has not come to know God, because God is love. By this the love of God was manifested among us: that God has sent his only begotten Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God thus loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God at any time. If we are loving one another, God is abiding in us, and his love has been perfected in us.

label: 1 John 4:13–16
text:
"Known and believed" translates two perfect-tense verbs together, egnōkamen kai pepisteukamen — a knowing and a believing both already accomplished and, right now, still standing, settled states rather than fresh acts of the moment.

"Testify" is martyroumen, formal witness-bearing vocabulary — the claim about Christ as "Saviour of the world" is presented as sworn testimony, not personal impression.

"Dwelleth in him" repeats menei one more time, still the letter's central verb for mutual, settled indwelling, applied here specifically to confession of Jesus as Son of God as its recognizable evidence.
translation: And we have seen and are testifying that the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God is abiding in him, and he in God. And we have come to know and have believed the love which God has in us. God is love, and the one who is abiding in love is abiding in God, and God is abiding in him.

label: 1 John 4:17–21
text:
"Made perfect" repeats teteleiōtai one final time — love reaching its intended goal specifically in producing "boldness" (parrēsian, the same civic-freedom word already used at 2:28 and 3:21) rather than dread, at the coming day of judgment.

"Casteth out" is exō ballei, present tense — an active, continuous, forceful expulsion, the same verb family used of driving something bodily out of a space, not a quiet fading.

"Torment" is kolasin, a term for judicial, penal punishment — fear itself is described as already carrying built-in punishment, functioning as a kind of sentence already being served rather than a mere unpleasant feeling.

"First loved" (prōtos ēgapēsen) fixes the entire logic of the chapter to a single point of origin — every subsequent love, God's toward us and ours toward one another, is traced back to this one prior, initiating act.
translation: In this love has been perfected with us, so that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, because just as that one is, so also are we in this world. There is no fear in love, but perfect love is casting out fear, because fear has punishment, and the one who fears has not been perfected in love. We are loving, because he first loved us. If anyone says, I love God, and is hating his brother, he is a liar; for the one who is not loving his brother, whom he has seen, is not able to love God, whom he has not seen. And this commandment we have from him: that the one who loves God should be loving his brother also.

label: 1 John 5:1–5
text:
"Born of God" is gegennētai, perfect tense — begotten and, right now, remaining in that begotten state, the same settled reality already used throughout chapter 3.

"Grievous" is bareiai, "heavy, weighty, burdensome" — the same adjective used elsewhere of a load too heavy to carry; God's commandments are declared, flatly, not to belong to that category.

"Overcometh" is nika, present tense — an ongoing, continuous state of victory, not a single battle already concluded and shelved.

"Victory" (nikē) appears here as a noun in its only New Testament use — the same root that gives Greek mythology its goddess of victory — and it is identified, without remainder, as "our faith" itself, the very thing believing, not some separate achievement added on top of it.
translation: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been begotten of God, and everyone who loves the one who begat also loves the one begotten of him. By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and are keeping his commandments. Because this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments, and his commandments are not heavy, because everyone who has been begotten of God overcomes the world; and this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. And who is the one overcoming the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

label: 1 John 5:6–8
text:
"Water and blood" most likely names two specific events bracketing Christ's public ministry — his baptism and his death — against a teaching that separated a divine "Christ" descending on the man Jesus at his baptism from the merely human Jesus who died; John insists the very same Jesus Christ was present, without division, at both.

"Beareth witness" (martyroun) is present participle — a continuous, ongoing testimony still being given, not a report closed and filed after a single occurrence.

The explicit Trinitarian wording sometimes printed here — "in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost" — is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and almost certainly a later scribal addition, not part of what John originally wrote; the earlier text simply names three witnesses on earth agreeing as one.

"Agree in one" translates eis to hen eisin, literally "are unto the one" — three separate testimonies converging, without conflict, on a single, unified verdict.
translation: This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ — not by the water only, but by the water and by the blood; and the Spirit is the one bearing witness, because the Spirit is the truth. Because there are three bearing witness: the Spirit, and the water, and the blood, and the three are unto the one.

label: 1 John 5:9–13
text:
"Witness" (martyria) governs this whole section, courtroom vocabulary for formal testimony sworn and received — believing is repeatedly framed as accepting a verdict already rendered, not arriving at a private opinion.

"Hath the witness in himself" describes an internal, personal possession of that testimony — the believer doesn't merely hear the verdict secondhand but carries it, afterward, as his own settled conviction.

"Made him a liar" is pseustēn pepoiēken auton, perfect tense — a completed act whose consequence still stands; unbelief is not framed as passive doubt but as an active verdict rendered against God's own truthfulness.

"Hath life" (echei tēn zōēn), present tense, ties eternal life to present possession of the Son as directly and simply as ownership of any object — a relationship either currently held or currently not, with no third category offered.
translation: If we receive the witness of men, the witness of God is greater, because this is the witness of God, that he has borne witness concerning his Son. The one who believes on the Son of God has the witness in himself. The one who does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the witness which God has borne concerning his Son. And this is the witness: that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. The one who has the Son has the life; the one who does not have the Son of God does not have the life. These things I have written to you so that you may know that you have eternal life, you who believe on the name of the Son of God.

label: 1 John 5:14–17
text:
"Confidence" repeats parrēsia a final time, the civic-boldness word running through the whole letter — open, unafraid access, here specifically applied to prayer offered "according to his will," a qualifying phrase that keeps the boldness from becoming presumption.

"Sin unto death" (hamartia pros thanaton) most likely describes a settled, final rejection of Christ rather than any single serious offense among believers — a category of sin John declines to instruct anyone to pray about, precisely because prayer presupposes a person still capable of turning.

"All unrighteousness is sin" is stated broadly and without exception, immediately followed by the narrower, deliberately unresolved category of sin "not unto death" — John draws a real line without drawing its exact location for his readers.
translation: And this is the confidence which we have toward him: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests which we have asked from him. If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, he will ask, and he will give him life, for those sinning not unto death. There is a sin unto death; I am not saying that he should make request concerning that. All unrighteousness is sin, and there is a sin not unto death.

label: 1 John 5:18–21
text:
"Keepeth himself" (tērei heauton) is read two ways by scholars — either the believer's own ongoing self-guarding, or, taking the participle "begotten of God" as a title for Christ himself, the Son actively keeping the believer safe; either reading places the wicked one's touch (haptetai, to lay hold of with hostile intent) at a real but unsuccessful distance.

"Lieth in wickedness" (en tō ponērō keitai) pictures the whole world reclining, at ease, comfortably at rest within the evil one's sphere — not merely oppressed by it but settled into it.

"Understanding" is dianoian, the actual faculty of comprehension — a capacity given, not merely information conveyed, so that the true God can genuinely be known rather than only described.

The abrupt closing command, "keep yourselves from idols," most likely names any false substitute set up in place of the true God just described — a fitting last word for a letter built, from its opening verses onward, around distinguishing the true from every plausible counterfeit.
translation: We know that everyone who has been begotten of God is not habitually sinning, but the one begotten of God keeps himself, and the evil one does not lay hold of him. We know that we are of God, and the whole world is lying in the power of the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come, and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This one is the true God and eternal life. Little children, guard yourselves from idols.
